title: NASA's Swift Telescope Falls to Earth After 22 Years
summary: One of NASA's most famous space telescopes has come down to Earth. The Swift Observatory plunged back into the atmosphere on Wednesday, ending a 22-year mission studying the universe's biggest explosions. The U.S. Space Force confirmed that Swift re-entered near Indonesia after tracking its sinking orbit. Intense solar activity over the past few years had dragged the telescope lower and lower. NASA had tried to save it. The space agency hired a private company, Katalyst Space, to rush together a rescue mission that would boost Swift's orbit. But the company's three-armed robotic craft ran into trouble after its July launch and came crashing down in September. It is not yet known how much of the nearly one-and-a-half-tonne spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere. NASA expects that some of the denser pieces survived the fall. Swift launched in 2004 on what was meant to be a two-year study of gamma-ray bursts and exploding stars. Instead, it kept working for 11 times longer than planned, observing thousands of these cosmic blasts and acting as a first responder for other telescopes, which could then look more closely. One famous catch was the afterglow of a giant gamma-ray burst called GRB 221009A. Now NASA is looking at how to protect another famous telescope: Hubble. Launched in 1990, Hubble is expected to come down by the mid-2030s, according to recent analyses. The agency is asking private companies for ideas about boosting Hubble's orbit, upgrading its systems, or guiding it to a controlled re-entry, and any mission would need to happen by 2032. "Hubble still has important science ahead of it," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement. "And we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible."
why_it_matters: Space telescopes help us see the universe, and losing one shows why scientists work to protect the ones we still have.

Solar activity means changes and storms on the Sun.
